aboutMePage.paragraphTwoContent: Through my diverse experience in law firms, NGOs, and public administrations in France and abroad, I have developed a disciplined working approach grounded in responsiveness, active listening, and a multidisciplinary perspective on legal issues.
aboutMePage.paragraphThreeContent: I have also developed expertise in immigration law, particularly since the Beirut port explosion, during which I was approached to assist many individuals with their procedures. Aware of the heavy workload and challenges they face, I aim to put my skills at their service to help them anticipate and overcome these obstacles.

tabsContent.immigrationTabContent:
Immigration Law

The firm assists individuals and businesses in all their procedures related to entering and residing in France.

  1. Visas, Residence Permits, and Legalization of Stay
    • Applications and renewals of residence permits
    • Work authorization requests
    • Legalization of stay for undocumented immigrants (traditional procedures and exceptional admission)
    • Assistance at the prefecture, preparation, and follow-up of applications
    • Legalization under “shortage occupations”
    • Change of status
  2. Family and Private Life
    • Family reunification
    • “Visitor” visas for retirees and freelancers
    • Family visas
    • Spouses of French or EU nationals
    • Partners under a civil union (PACS)
    • Resident cards (10 years)
  3. Support for all subcategories of the “Talent Passport” residence permit
    • Skilled employee
    • Recruitment in an innovative company
    • Highly qualified employment
    • Employee on assignment
    • Researcher
    • Business creation
    • Innovative project recognized by a public body
    • Investor
    • Corporate officer
    • Artistic and cultural profession
    • Person of international renown
  4. Naturalization and Citizenship
    • Applications for naturalization / acquisition of French nationality
    • Appeals against postponement or rejection decisions in naturalization applications
  5. Litigation and Appeals
    • Appeals against prefectural postponement/rejection decisions
    • Appeals against visa refusals
  6. Consular Relations
    • Procedures with Consulates in France: obtaining certificates of custom, proof of name change, and drafting of legal opinions in family and inheritance law for states with Muslim or mixed legal systems (e.g., Lebanon).
  7. Support for Foreign Entrepreneurs

    We support foreign entrepreneurs and investors in their business projects in France, whether to start an activity, expand an existing structure, or invest in the French economy. Personalized support is offered for your installation, with follow-up from your arrival in France (connections with chambers of commerce, specialized economic bodies).

    Our support includes:

    • Review of your project and guidance towards the most appropriate procedure (entrepreneur visa, Talent Passport, business creator or investor)
    • Full preparation of your file: drafting the business plan, financial justifications, proof of activity or investment
    • Submission of the application to the competent authorities (consulate or prefecture)
    • Monitoring of procedures and communication with relevant administrations (DREETS, Ministry of the Interior, prefectures)
tabsContent.businessTabContent:
Business Law

Starting a business in France as a non-resident is a tremendous opportunity: a dynamic market, attractive public support (such as the French Tech program), and a secure legal framework. However, the administrative, tax, and social processes can be complex.

We support you at every stage of your entrepreneurial project in France:

  • Company formation (SAS, SARL, EURL, etc.)
  • Drafting and adaptation of bylaws
  • Company registration and administrative formalities
  • Assistance in anticipating the tax consequences of your establishment and optimizing your strategy to avoid double taxation under international treaties
  • Support for foreign entrepreneurs in their procedures from abroad, taking into account specific challenges related to compliance and anti-money laundering/combating the financing of terrorism
tabsContent.foreignBusinessTabContent:
Foreign Businesses Law

We support foreign entrepreneurs with their procedures from abroad, taking into account the challenges related to culture, development, and the promotion of their expertise. We also assist with the recruitment of foreign employees from their countries of origin.

content.appointmentDifficultyPubPreviewTitle: Difficulties Getting an Appointment at the Prefecture: What Are Your Options?
content.appointmentDifficultyPubPreviewContent: You need to apply to the prefecture or sub-prefecture of your place of residence for a residence permit, but you cannot get an appointment online. Here is what you can do.
content.appointmentDifficultyPubContent:
Difficulties getting an appointment at the prefecture: what are your options?

You need to apply to the prefecture or sub-prefecture of your place of residence to submit a residence permit application, but the process seems complicated. You try to book an appointment online without success, and you may even be considering paying intermediaries who sell appointments at exorbitant prices, even though their activity is illegal.

Rest assured, you are not alone in this situation. In the Île-de-France region, this problem affects several prefectures and sub-prefectures in particular.

What can you do?

  1. Write to the prefecture

    You can inform the prefecture, by letter, that it has been impossible to obtain an appointment and ask to be summoned. This option has its limits, however, since the prefecture may simply ask you to try again online.

  2. Apply to the administrative court on an urgent basis (référé)

    You can ask the court to order the prefecture to issue you a summons so that you can submit your file. To do this, you must provide evidence of your unsuccessful attempts (screenshots, reminder emails sent to the prefecture, and so on).

We can assist you with this procedure before the administrative court. We also handle the entire process: preparing your file, dealing with the prefecture, and following up on the examination of your application until the administration's final decision.
content.jobsInTensionPubPreviewContent: On 22 May 2025, a new list of shortage occupations was published under the law of 26 January 2024 (the Darmanin law). It allows certain undocumented workers to regularise their status through employment.
content.jobsInTensionPubContent:
Shortage occupations 2025: regularisation through work

On 22 May 2025, a new list of shortage occupations (métiers en tension) was published under the law of 26 January 2024 on shortage occupations, known as the Darmanin law. This law allows certain foreign nationals without legal status to regularise their residence through work. The list of occupations is updated by region and is available on Légifrance.

The order of 21 May 2025 updates the occupations for which:

  • an employer can recruit a foreign worker without the administration objecting on the grounds of the local employment situation;
  • an employee without a residence permit can apply for regularisation on their own.

1. Conditions for regularisation

The employee must meet all of the following conditions:

  • have worked as an employee for at least 12 months, consecutive or not, during the last 24 months, in an occupation on the shortage list;
  • hold, at the time of the application, a job on that list, which varies by region;
  • prove uninterrupted residence in France for at least 3 years.

2. Which occupations are covered?

The full list is available region by region on Légifrance. It can be estimated to include dozens, and in some cases more than a hundred, occupations, depending on specialisations, qualification levels and regional needs.

The most represented sectors include:

  • construction;
  • industry;
  • hotels and catering;
  • agriculture;
  • transport;
  • certain technical or digital roles.

3. Disqualifying criterion

The residence permit cannot be issued if the foreign national has been the subject of a conviction, incapacity or forfeiture recorded in bulletin no. 2 of the criminal record.

The prefect retains discretion and may refuse regularisation taking into account social and family integration, respect for public order, integration, and adherence to the values of the Republic (article L. 412-7 of the CESEDA).

4. Care in preparing the file

The file must include:

  • an employment contract or a promise of employment;
  • proof of presence in France for at least 3 years;
  • any evidence of lasting integration: housing, professional and social integration, stability.

Regularisation through work remains a demanding procedure. It is strongly recommended to be assisted by a lawyer specialising in immigration law.
content.obtainingFrenchNationalityPubPreviewCont: Acquiring French nationality by naturalisation (the procedure by decree) is subject to precise conditions and a regulated administrative process. Here are the steps, from eligibility to appeals.
content.obtainingFrenchNationalityPubContent:
Obtaining French nationality through naturalisation

Acquiring French nationality by naturalisation (the procedure by decree) is subject to precise conditions and a regulated administrative procedure, in accordance with articles 21 and following of the Civil Code (article L110-6 of the CESEDA). Our firm assists you at every stage to maximise your chances of success.

1. Preliminary step: checking the eligibility conditions

To be eligible for naturalisation, you must in principle have resided in France for at least 5 years. This period can be reduced, or even waived, in certain cases (an outstanding academic record, particular talents, services rendered to France, and so on). For example, the 5 year period is reduced to 2 years for people who have successfully completed 2 years of higher education leading to a French degree or to admission to the next year of study.

The applicant must also:

  • have a command of the French language,
  • have sufficient knowledge of French history, culture and institutions,
  • be legally resident in France,
  • not have committed certain crimes or offences.

2. Next step: preparing and submitting the file

The naturalisation application is made using a form available on the government website or from the prefecture. It must be accompanied by all the required supporting documents.

  • Submitting the file: in France, it is submitted to the prefecture of the place of residence; abroad, it must be sent to the consular authority.
  • Examination of the application: the prefecture carries out an investigation, may request additional documents, and organises an individual interview.

3. Final step: the decision

  • Acceptance: if the decision is favourable, the applicant is invited to attend the naturalisation ceremony, generally within 6 months.
  • Postponement (ajournement): even if the application is admissible, the prefect or the Minister of the Interior may postpone it. The decision, which must state its reasons, may set a waiting period (often two years) or impose certain conditions. It can be challenged before the administrative court.
  • Refusal: the application may be refused, in which case two avenues of appeal are open:
  • Request for re-examination: the applicant can ask for the file to be examined again by sending a reasoned letter of appeal, by registered post with acknowledgement of receipt, within two months of notification of the refusal.
  • Hierarchical appeal: if the re-examination is rejected, a hierarchical appeal can be lodged with the Minister of the Interior, again by registered post with acknowledgement of receipt, within two months. The administration then has four months to respond.
  • Court appeal: if the administrative appeals are rejected, or if no response is received within the time limit, the applicant can bring the case before the competent administrative court. This appeal must be lodged within two months of the explicit or implicit rejection decision.

Appeals and assistance

Appeals must be properly reasoned and lodged within the legal time limits. The assistance of a lawyer is a key asset in securing the procedure and strengthening the chances of a favourable outcome.
content.seasonalEmployeeVisaPubPreviewTitle: The Seasonal Worker Visa: A Strict Framework, Often a Source of Difficulties
content.seasonalEmployeeVisaPubPreviewContent: The "seasonal worker" residence permit allows foreign nationals to come and work in France, but only for part of the year. Behind this attractive title lies a very strict legal framework.
content.seasonalEmployeeVisaPubContent:
The seasonal worker visa: a strict framework, often a source of difficulties

The "seasonal worker" residence permit allows foreign nationals to come and work in France, but only for part of the year. Behind this attractive title lies a very strict legal framework, which frequently creates obstacles for the workers concerned as well as for their employers.

I. A residence permit that is limited by nature

This permit is intended exclusively for foreign nationals recruited for seasonal jobs:

  • agriculture
  • tourism
  • hotels
  • catering
  • wine growing
  • and so on

The permit allows the holder to work for up to six months per year, but it does not give any right to permanent residence. The holder must keep their main residence in their country of origin and undertakes to return there at the end of each seasonal assignment. In addition, a new work authorisation must be requested for each contract, which makes the administrative procedures even heavier.

  1. The main difficulties for seasonal workers
    • 1. Very long recruitment times

      A large proportion of seasonal workers are recruited from Morocco. However, the procedures carried out through the OFII in that country can take more than six months, making the process extremely complex for farmers, who depend on labour being available quickly.

    • 2. Overwhelmed prefectures

      Even once in France, workers often have to wait more than a year to obtain their residence permit, whereas their authorised stay is only six months. As a result, many have to leave the country before their permit is issued, then start the whole process again the following year, a situation that is both absurd and exhausting.

    • 3. Fraudulent practices and serious abuse

      The system also opens the door to certain abuses. Several unscrupulous companies or intermediaries produce false documents for workers (such as EDF electricity bills) in order to obtain the authorisations.

      Once in France, some seasonal workers find themselves exploited in degrading conditions, dependent on employers who take advantage of their precarious administrative situation.

  2. A frozen status: no change of category possible
    • Another major difficulty: no change of status is permitted. A seasonal worker cannot move to an "employee" (salarié) permit that would allow them to work full time and reside in France on a lasting basis, even if they are perfectly integrated and hold a stable job.
    • The only exception is family reunification or private and family life, but this remains strictly regulated and must not be used to circumvent the law, at the risk of being classified as a sham marriage, which is severely punished.

II. A status in need of reform?

Between administrative delays, the impossibility of settling in France, and the risks of exploitation, the seasonal worker status now appears ill suited to economic and human realities.

Many employers, particularly in agriculture, are calling for simpler procedures, while associations are campaigning for better regulation to protect workers.

In a context of labour shortages and intense debate on labour migration, the question of reforming the seasonal worker status may well come back on the table soon.
content.frenchEntrepreneurVisaPubPreviewContent: Every year, many foreign nationals choose France to create or develop an independent business activity. The entrepreneur visa represents...
content.frenchEntrepreneurVisaPubContent:
THE FRENCH ENTREPRENEUR VISA

Conditions, procedure and 2026 updates

Every year, many foreign nationals choose France to create or develop an independent business activity. The entrepreneur visa represents a genuine opportunity, but it is subject to strict requirements: the project must be genuine, serious, viable, and suited to the applicant's profile. This article reviews the two available residence permits, the procedure to follow, and the new supporting documents required since the order (arrêté) of 13 May 2026.

I. TWO RESIDENCE PERMITS FOR ENTREPRENEURS

1. The “Entrepreneur / Liberal Profession” permit (Article L. 421-5 of the CESEDA)

This permit is intended for applicants wishing to carry out, in France, an activity that is:

  • commercial;
  • craft-based (artisanale);
  • industrial;
  • agricultural;
  • a liberal profession;
  • or carried out as a sole trader (entreprise individuelle).

French law sets no minimum investment amount. The applicant must nonetheless demonstrate sufficient funds to launch the activity, and that the activity will generate income at least equivalent to the full-time gross annual minimum wage (SMIC) — €22,404.20 as of 1 June 2026.

The permit is generally issued for one year and may then be renewed if the activity is genuinely carried out and remains economically viable.

2. The “Talent – Project Holder” permit (formerly “Talent – Business Creator”)

Following decree n° 2025-539 of 13 June 2025, the former “business creator,” “innovative project,” and “investor” categories were merged into a single “Talent – Project Holder” permit (Article L. 421-16, 3° of the CESEDA). This permit remains more advantageous than the “Entrepreneur” permit, as it can be issued for a period of up to four years.

It nonetheless requires:

  • a master's-level degree, or five years of comparable professional experience;
  • a genuine and serious business creation project;
  • an investment of at least €30,000;
  • sufficient personal resources, at least equivalent to the annual SMIC.

The applicant's spouse may also be granted a “Talent (family)” permit authorizing them to work in France.

II. WHAT CHANGES IN 2026: NEW REQUIRED DOCUMENTS

The order (arrêté) of 13 May 2026 clarified the list of supporting documents required for an application for an opinion on the economic viability of the non-salaried activity, requested for the “Entrepreneur/Liberal Profession” permit (Article L. 421-5 of the CESEDA).

The documents common to all applications now include:

  • a copy of the passport;
  • where applicable, proof of compliance with the regulatory conditions for practicing the intended profession or activity;
  • if the activity is already registered, a registration certificate from the French national companies register (RNE) dated less than six months.

Additional documents are required depending on the situation:

  • Creating an activity: presentation of the project and business plan, proof of a positive account balance, documents relating to premises and equipment, proof of qualifications or experience;
  • Joining an existing company: a tax status statement (P237), the company's articles of association or proof of appointment, and an employment contract or accounting records showing remuneration at least equivalent to the SMIC.

Practical tip: applicants are advised to obtain the criminal record extract and its certified translation as early as possible, since these steps can significantly delay the filing of the application when the applicant resides abroad.

III. MAIN STEPS OF THE PROCEDURE

The applicant must prepare a file including, in particular:

  • a business plan;
  • a market study;
  • financial projections;
  • proof of financing;
  • diplomas and professional experience;
  • the draft articles of association (statuts) of the company;
  • proof of business address (domiciliation).

The application is filed with the French consulate where the applicant resides abroad, or with the relevant French authority in the case of a change of status while already in France.

IV. MISTAKES THAT UNDERMINE AN APPLICATION

1. An insufficiently detailed project

Simply forming a company or a micro-enterprise is not enough. The authorities verify that the activity is credible, funded, and capable of generating income.

2. Confusion between the two permits

Many applicants apply for a “Talent” permit without holding the required €30,000, or submit an “Entrepreneur” application without demonstrating the economic viability of the project.

3. Unrealistic financial projections

Projected revenue that is announced without supporting contracts, clientele, or a serious market study can lead to a refusal.

4. Regulated activities

Certain professions require a diploma, an administrative authorization, or registration with a professional body. Setting up a company does not allow these requirements to be bypassed.

V. FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

How long does it take to process an entrepreneur visa application?

Processing times vary depending on the competent consulate or prefecture and on how complete the file is. Applicants are advised to start preparing the file several months before the intended departure date, particularly to gather the economic viability opinion and, where applicable, the translated criminal record.

Do I have to invest €30,000?

No. This amount only applies to the “Talent – Project Holder” permit. The “Entrepreneur/Liberal Profession” permit imposes no legal minimum amount, but requires proof of sufficient funds and a viable activity capable of generating income at least equivalent to the SMIC.

Can I bring my spouse and children?

The holder of a “Talent – Project Holder” permit can have their spouse granted a “Talent (family)” permit. For the “Entrepreneur/Liberal Profession” permit, family members' arrival follows the ordinary family reunification rules, subject to meeting resource and housing requirements.

What can I do if my application is refused?

A refusal can be challenged through an informal or hierarchical appeal to the authorities, and then through a contentious appeal before the competent administrative court, within two months of notification of the decision. Meeting this deadline and precisely substantiating the appeal are essential.

WHY WORK WITH A LAWYER

The entrepreneur visa represents a genuine opportunity to build a business activity in France. However, registering a company does not automatically create a right of residence: the success of the application depends on the coherence of the project, its financing, and the applicant's ability to prove that the activity will allow them to support themselves durably.

Maître Sarah Haidar supports her clients at every stage: assessing the situation, choosing the most suitable permit, preparing the economic viability file, drafting the business plan, and following through until the permit is granted — or, in the event of a refusal, through the contentious appeal. We work in French, English, and Arabic, and regularly assists Lebanese, Syrian, Egyptian, and Gulf clients with their relocation to France.
